Senses.Explanation: The normal Chan use is a title for the person who teaches and presides over a monastic community. Linji Yixuan says that meeting a great teacher enabled him to recognize “the old masters under heaven” (天下老和尚), and Yezhu Fusheng introduces the named Cloth-Bag Master of Mingzhou. Nanyue Huairang says that he comes from Master An of Songshan, while the Admonitions of the Chan Grove introduces an authority with “Master Wuzu Fayan said” (五祖演和尚曰). Xiaotang Chaoyuan's portrait verse addresses Master Sanmei by title and calls him a model for people and gods. Direct address changes English capitalization and syntax but not the referent. Huike begs Bodhidharma, “I only beg you, Master, to show compassion” (惟願和尚慈悲). Huang Tingjian asks Huitang Zuxin why he has such an urgently caring heart. Guishan Lingyou turns Baizhang Huaihai's question back by asking Baizhang to say it, and Zhaozhou Congshen thanks Nanquan Puyuan for his instruction. Huangbo Xiyun can gather “all the old masters under heaven” in one place. Across these forms, the Chan deviation is institutional and documentary: the title identifies named people who teach, are questioned and answered in public encounters, and are cited as authorities and heads of communities.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 52,209 occurrences in 441 texts. Render direct address as capitalized “Master”; in narrative prose use a definite lower-case rendering, a named form such as “Master Bodhidharma,” or “abbot” only where the office is explicit. Direct address is grammatical variation, not a separate sense. Xuefeng Yicun's embedded address “monk-fellows” (和尚子) is a separate compound, recorded here as family evidence rather than standalone depth. The ordination-preceptor role is separately attested below and must not be merged into this teaching relation.

Linji is the exact speaker, not an addressee or section subject.

Senses.Explanation: In ordination accounts the same title names the person from whom someone receives the precepts, a different office from the teaching master. Tianze Neng titles a portrait verse “Praise of the ordination preceptor” (得戒和尚贊) and praises that figure for rigorously maintaining the Vinaya, while He Yizi separates “listening to the teaching under Teacher Buye” from “receiving the precepts from Preceptor Yulin” (聽教於不夜天師、受戒於玉林和尚). The office is also named directly: Jie Weizhou says that Preceptor Ruo'an of Louze was asked to serve as the preceptor from whom the precepts were received (乞漏澤箬菴和尚為得戒師), while Zhufeng Huanmin's incense verse honors a “preceptor from whom the precepts were received” (得戒和尚) alongside distinct tonsure teachers. This is a precept-family deployment of the title: it identifies the human conferrer in an ordination relation, not merely a respectful reading of the teaching-master sense.
Senses.Note: Do not infer this sense from every occurrence of “precept/Master Jie” (戒和尚). In early lamp records that sequence often means “Master Jie,” where Jie is a personal name, especially Wuzu Jie. Huanglong Huinan raises “Master Wuzu Jie” (五祖戒和尚) in an unrelated letter-delivery case; this is a personal-name use, not ordination. Assign the preceptor sense only when receiving or conferring precepts, the explicit title “preceptor from whom the precepts were received” (得戒和尚), or an equivalent role statement supplies the relation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 得戒和尚贊稽首如是，佛門宗匠，悟大總持，纔得心放。華峰入室，當仁不讓，嚴淨毘尼，楚地惟上。

Tianze is the exact author of the verse; the preceptor is its titled subject. Tianze Neng is not yet on the roster.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉五祖戒和尚。為智門馳書到德山。圓明接得乃問。這箇是智門底。那箇是專使底。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huanglong Huinan, in his Recorded Sayings (黃龍慧南禪師語錄), raises a letter-delivery case involving Wuzu Jie and names him Master Wuzu Jie.
